notes.label: osteoporosis
notes.detail: Repeated forward bending of the loaded spine is the classic mechanism of vertebral compression fracture in fragile bone. This is not a tolerance question that can be modified around — it is the movement direction to avoid.

notes.label: history of falls
notes.detail: Unsupported balance work is the point of the exercise and also its risk; the manual requires confirming the person can recover balance with lower-limb strategies before prescribing any unsupported level.
notes.modification: Stay at the supported level until recovery strategies are confirmed. Work beside a solid bench or kitchen counter, never a chair that slides.

notes.label: history of falls

notes.label: osteoporosis
notes.detail: Not the exercise itself but its failure mode: a fall from single-leg stance in someone with fragile bone is the injury the whole programme exists to prevent.
notes.modification: Keep a hand on a solid counter at every level, including the 30-second one. The balance benefit survives light fingertip support; a fractured wrist does not.

notes.label: uncontrolled hypertension
notes.detail: The piked position puts the head below the heart repeatedly.
notes.modification: Fewer, slower reaches with the hands elevated.

notes.label: uncontrolled hypertension
notes.detail: Rapid repeated changes between standing and head-down floor positions at high effort are a blood-pressure and dizziness double load.
notes.modification: Level 1-2 only (no jump levels), a full breath's pause at the crouch before rising, and stop for any light-headedness. With BP that is not well controlled, do not prescribe this entry at all — the mountain-climber step-through covers the conditioning goal without the posture change.

notes.label: uncontrolled hypertension
notes.detail: High-cadence whole-body work raises blood pressure sharply.
notes.modification: Shorter intervals at a talking pace; stop for a pounding head or dizziness.

notes.label: uncontrolled hypertension
notes.detail: Sustained overhead arm work with jumping raises blood pressure more than leg work alone.
notes.modification: Keep the hands at shoulder height rather than overhead, and keep intervals short.

notes.label: uncontrolled hypertension
notes.detail: Head-below-heart positioning plus hard intervals is a double blood-pressure load.
notes.modification: Use the slow step-through version with the hands elevated on a step; keep intervals short.

bone.display_name: Walking Intervals (Aerobic Interval Training on Foot)

notes.label: uncontrolled hypertension
notes.detail: Interval work deliberately pushes the heart rate higher than steady walking does, which is the intensity band that needs clearance when there is cardiovascular disease.
notes.modification: Confirm medical clearance before the brisk blocks. Keep the brisk effort at "can still speak in short sentences" rather than breathless, and stop for chest tightness, unusual breathlessness or light-headedness.

notes.label: cardiovascular disease
notes.detail: The manual's stop rule: dizziness, chest pain or shortness of breath during exercise means stop and contact the doctor.
notes.modification: Keep to a pace that allows conversation (talk test); stop on any dizziness, chest pain or breathlessness and review with the doctor.

notes.label: history of falls
notes.detail: Unsupported balance work is the point of the exercise and also its risk; the manual requires confirming the person can recover balance with lower-limb strategies before prescribing any unsupported level.
notes.modification: Stay at the supported level until recovery strategies are confirmed. Work beside a solid bench or kitchen counter, never a chair that slides.

notes.label: osteoporosis
notes.detail: The side bend and the trunk turn take the spine towards its end range in bending and rotation. Unloaded and small they are low risk, but end-range flexion is still the direction to respect in fragile bone.
notes.modification: Keep the side bend and the turn small and slow — a quarter of the available range, not the end of it — or leave both out and keep the wrist, shoulder, ankle and hip circles, which is most of the warm-up anyway.

notes.label: uncontrolled hypertension
notes.detail: Large-muscle resistance work raises blood pressure transiently, and rising hard from the bottom invites a held breath.
notes.modification: Breathe out on the way up. Stand up smoothly rather than straining, and stop for dizziness or head pressure on standing.

notes.label: uncontrolled hypertension
notes.detail: Resistance work raises blood pressure transiently and hard repetitions invite breath holding.
notes.modification: Breathe out on the push up and stop the set while it is still comfortable.

notes.label: hypertension
notes.detail: A whole-body isometric hold drives a pressor response for as long as it lasts, and holding the breath against it raises blood pressure sharply. The same warning that applies to the wall squat applies here.
notes.modification: Keep holds to 20 seconds, breathe audibly throughout so the breath cannot be held, and rest fully between them. Do not prescribe while blood pressure is uncontrolled or unmeasured.

notes.label: history of falls
notes.detail: The narrow split stance with the weight travelling forwards is the least stable strength movement in this catalogue, and it is done standing.
notes.modification: Keep a hand on a solid counter for every repetition until the movement is confident; never use a chair that can slide. Do not prescribe unsupported until standing balance has been confirmed.

notes.label: uncontrolled hypertension
notes.detail: Large-muscle work raises blood pressure transiently, and repeatedly standing up from a low position can provoke a light head.
notes.modification: Breathe out on the way up, come up smoothly, and stop for dizziness rather than pushing through it.

notes.label: history of falls
notes.detail: Unsupported balance work is the point of the exercise and also its risk; the manual requires confirming the person can recover balance with lower-limb strategies before prescribing any unsupported level.
notes.modification: Stay at the supported level until recovery strategies are confirmed. Work beside a solid bench or kitchen counter, never a chair that slides.

notes.label: uncontrolled hypertension
notes.detail: Resistance work raises blood pressure transiently, and straining against a hard repetition with a held breath raises it sharply.
notes.modification: Breathe out on the push. Stop the set while it is still comfortable rather than grinding out a last repetition, and stop for head pressure or dizziness.

notes.label: uncontrolled hypertension
notes.detail: Maximal effort against gravity spikes blood pressure.
notes.modification: Sub-maximal heights, long rests, exhale on the drive.

notes.label: uncontrolled hypertension
notes.detail: Near-maximal repetitions are commonly done with a held breath, which produces a sharp transient rise in blood pressure.
notes.modification: Breathe out on every push and stop the set two repetitions before failure. Do not prescribe this until blood pressure is known to be managed.

notes.label: uncontrolled hypertension
notes.detail: Any resistance work raises blood pressure transiently, and breath-holding against effort raises it sharply.
notes.modification: Breathe out on the push and in on the lower; never hold the breath. Stop for head pressure, throbbing or dizziness. Confirm blood pressure is being managed before adding the second set.

notes.label: hypertension
notes.detail: Sustained isometric contraction drives a pressor response — blood pressure climbs for as long as the hold lasts, and climbs much higher if the breath is held against it. This book states plainly that isometric exercises should be avoided by anyone with high blood pressure.
notes.modification: Keep holds to 15-20 seconds, breathe out audibly throughout so the breath cannot be held, and rest fully between holds. Do not prescribe at all while blood pressure is uncontrolled or unmeasured, or in pregnancy with raised blood pressure — use bodyweight-squat repetitions instead, which do not sustain the contraction.

notes.label: knee pain
notes.detail: Repeated maximal landings through a painful knee is a flare generator, and the squat ladder below this rung covers every strength goal without the impact.

notes.label: osteoarthritis
notes.detail: The Otago manual instructs people with rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis or other painful conditions to work in a pain-free range.
notes.modification: Reduce range until the movement is pain-free rather than reducing frequency; stop if muscle pain does not settle afterwards.

notes.label: knee osteoarthritis
notes.detail: Repeated loaded knee flexion is the movement most likely to flare an arthritic knee.
notes.modification: Raise the seat height (a cushion works) to reduce the depth, and keep within a pain-free range.

notes.label: knee pain
notes.detail: The crouch and the jump landings both load bent knees at speed.
notes.modification: Level 1 only, stepping in and out; skip the jump levels entirely.

notes.label: knee pain
notes.detail: Repeated single-leg landings load one knee at a time at cadence.
notes.modification: March instead of hop; height of the knee matters more than the bounce.

notes.label: knee pain
notes.detail: Every landing is a ground-reaction spike through the knees, dozens of times a minute.
notes.modification: Use the step-out version, or halve the interval length and land consciously softly.

notes.label: knee pain
notes.detail: Every landing loads a split stance through the front knee.
notes.modification: Keep the split short and the hop minimal, or use the step-through version.

notes.label: knee pain
notes.detail: Walking faster increases the load through the knee and hip with every step, and the total step count rises with the session length.
notes.modification: Lengthen the easy blocks rather than shortening the walk, keep to flat even ground, and check the shoes. Reduce the number of pairs if joints are sore the following day.

notes.label: knee osteoarthritis
notes.detail: Descending stairs loads the knee more than ascending.
notes.modification: Descend one step at a time leading with the same leg, holding the rail; reduce flights before reducing frequency.

notes.label: osteoarthritis

notes.label: knee pain
notes.detail: Knee compression rises steeply with depth, and the bottom of a deep squat is where patellofemoral pain is usually provoked.
notes.modification: Reduce the DEPTH, not the frequency — stay in the range that is pain-free even if that is only a few centimetres, and build repetitions there before going lower.

notes.label: knee pain
notes.detail: A lunge puts most of the body weight through one knee at a bent angle, which is a substantially bigger single-knee load than a two-legged squat.
notes.modification: Shorten the depth first and the stride second, and keep the front knee stacked over the heel. If a painful knee cannot do a shallow lunge comfortably, stay on bodyweight-squat — this movement is not a required rung.

notes.modification: Reduce range until the movement is pain-free rather than reducing frequency; stop if muscle pain does not settle afterwards.

notes.label: knee pain
notes.detail: The whole position rests body weight directly on the kneecaps against the floor.
notes.modification: Double the mat or kneel on a folded towel. If pressure on the kneecap still hurts, do not modify this — stay at the wall version, which loads no knee at all.

notes.label: knee pain
notes.detail: A sustained hold keeps the kneecap loaded continuously, which some painful knees tolerate better than repetitions and some tolerate far worse.
notes.modification: Hold higher up the wall so the knee bend is shallow. Shallow and pain-free beats deep and sore; depth can come later or not at all.
